fig.alt: Schematic with animated energy flowing from hot reservoir through engine to work and cold reservoir.

check.q: An engine takes 1000 J from the hot reservoir and rejects 700 J. Its efficiency is:

sections.md:
Run an engine backwards and you get a **refrigerator**: it takes heat Q₂ from a cold region, needs work W done on it, and dumps Q₁ = Q₂ + W to the hot surroundings. That's why the coils at the back of your fridge are warm.

Inside, a refrigerant gas is compressed (gets hot), releases heat to the room through the coils, then expands suddenly through a valve (cools sharply) and absorbs heat from the food compartment.

**Coefficient of performance**: **α = Q₂/W = Q₂/(Q₁ − Q₂)**. Unlike efficiency, α can be greater than 1 — good fridges move several joules of heat per joule of electricity. The star rating on an Indian air-conditioner is based on this kind of figure.

A **heat pump** is the same machine used to warm a room: it pumps heat *in* from colder outside air.

The first law says energy is conserved. But it allows things we never see: a cup of cold tea spontaneously heating up by cooling the room; a ship running on heat extracted from sea water alone. The **second law** forbids these.

**Kelvin–Planck statement**: no process is possible whose *sole* result is the absorption of heat from a reservoir and its complete conversion into work. (No engine can be 100% efficient.)

**Clausius statement**: no process is possible whose *sole* result is the transfer of heat from a colder object to a hotter one. (A fridge needs work.)

The two statements are equivalent: violating one lets you violate the other.

**Reversible and irreversible processes**: a process is **reversible** if it can be retraced so that both the system and the surroundings return exactly to their original states. Real processes are **irreversible**: friction, free expansion of gas into a vacuum, mixing of milk in tea, heat flowing across a finite temperature difference. Reversible processes are idealisations — quasi-static and with no dissipation.

check.q: Which statement is a form of the second law?
options: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed
Heat cannot by itself flow from a colder to a hotter body
Systems in equilibrium with a third are in equilibrium with each other
check.why: This is the Clausius statement; the others are the first law, the ideal-gas equation and the zeroth law.

sections.h: The Carnot engine: the best possible
sections.md:
In 1824 the French engineer **Sadi Carnot** asked: what is the most efficient engine possible between two temperatures T₁ (hot) and T₂ (cold)? His answer: a **reversible** engine working in the **Carnot cycle** of four steps:

1. **Isothermal expansion** at T₁, absorbing Q₁.
2. **Adiabatic expansion** from T₁ to T₂.
3. **Isothermal compression** at T₂, rejecting Q₂.
4. **Adiabatic compression** from T₂ back to T₁.

For an ideal gas, Q₂/Q₁ = T₂/T₁, so the **Carnot efficiency** is

**η = 1 − T₂/T₁** (temperatures in kelvin)

**Carnot's theorem**: (a) no engine between two given temperatures can be more efficient than a Carnot engine; (b) the Carnot efficiency doesn't depend on the working substance.

To get a better engine, raise T₁ or lower T₂. That's why modern power stations use very high-pressure, superheated steam. Efficiency would reach 100% only if T₂ = 0 K — which can't be reached.

**Did you know?** The Carnot result even gives a way to define temperature that doesn't depend on any substance at all — the thermodynamic Kelvin scale.

check.q: A Carnot engine works between 500 K and 300 K. Its efficiency is:

workedExamples.q: 1 mole of an ideal gas at 300 K expands isothermally to twice its volume. Find the work done and the heat absorbed. (R = 8.31 J/mol K, ln 2 = 0.693)
steps: Isothermal ideal gas: ΔU = 0 so Q = W.

workedExamples.q: A gas at constant pressure 2 × 10⁵ Pa expands from 0.01 m³ to 0.03 m³ while absorbing 10 kJ of heat. Find ΔU.
A refrigerator keeps its inside at 0 °C (273 K) in a room at 27 °C (300 K). Find the maximum (Carnot) coefficient of performance.
steps: α = T₂/(T₁ − T₂) for a Carnot refrigerator.

workedExamples.q: A Carnot engine of efficiency 25% has a cold reservoir at 27 °C. By how much must the hot reservoir temperature rise to make the efficiency 40%?

summary: Thermodynamics describes systems by macroscopic variables P, V, T, U.
Zeroth law: thermal equilibrium is transitive — defines temperature.
Heat is energy in transit due to temperature difference (Joule, Rumford).
Internal energy is a state variable; heat and work are not.
First law: ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW; work by gas = PΔV = area under P–V curve.
Cp − Cv = R; γ = Cp/Cv (5/3 monatomic, 7/5 diatomic).
Isothermal: PV = const, ΔU = 0, Q = W = μRT ln(V₂/V₁).
Adiabatic: Q = 0, PVᵞ = const; expanding gas cools.
Isochoric: W = 0; isobaric: W = PΔV.
Heat engine efficiency η = W/Q₁ = 1 − Q₂/Q₁.
Refrigerator COP α = Q₂/W; can exceed 1.
Second law (Kelvin–Planck, Clausius): no 100% engine; no unaided heat flow from cold to hot.
Real processes are irreversible (friction, free expansion, mixing).
Carnot efficiency 1 − T₂/T₁ is the maximum between two temperatures.

glossary.d: Infinitely slow process through equilibrium states
Body so large its temperature doesn't change when heat is exchanged
Heat removed per unit work for a refrigerator
Reversible cycle of two isothermal and two adiabatic steps

rd-school-c11-physics-c.ch11-thermodynam.title: Thermodynamics — Part 2: Derivations, P–V Diagrams & Every Exercise Type
rd-school-c11-physics-c.ch11-thermodynam.subtitle: Work as area, the adiabatic formula from scratch, free expansion, and fully solved exam problems

sections.h: Work as area: reading a P–V diagram like an engineer
sections.md:
In Part 1 you met ΔW = PΔV. When pressure changes during the process, split the change into tiny steps dV, each doing work P dV, and add them up: **W = ∫ P dV**, the **area under the curve** on a P–V diagram between V₁ and V₂.

Three rules make P–V questions easy:

1. **Moving right (expansion)** → work done *by* the gas is positive. Moving left (compression) → negative.
2. **Vertical line (isochoric)** → zero area, zero work.
3. **Closed loop (cycle)** → net work = area enclosed. **Clockwise** loop: net work done by the gas (an engine). **Anticlockwise**: net work done on the gas (a refrigerator).

Because the area depends on the path, two processes between the same initial and final states can involve different work and different heat — yet the **same ΔU**, since U is a state variable. This is the cleanest way to show that heat and work are not state variables.

**Example in words:** take a gas from state A to state C either via B (first at constant pressure, then at constant volume) or via D (first constant volume, then constant pressure). The rectangle under the higher-pressure route is larger, so more work is done along it, and therefore more heat must be absorbed — but ΔU is identical.

fig.alt: A point travelling clockwise round a rectangular cycle on a P-V diagram, with the enclosed area glowing.

check.q: A gas is taken round a cycle that appears anticlockwise on a P–V diagram. Then:
options: Net work is done by the gas
Net work is done on the gas
check.why: For an anticlockwise loop the compression happens at higher pressure than the expansion, so the surroundings do net work on the gas.

sections.h: Deriving the isothermal and adiabatic results
sections.md:
**Isothermal work.** For μ moles at constant T, P = μRT/V. Then W = ∫ P dV from V₁ to V₂ = μRT ∫ dV/V = **μRT ln(V₂/V₁)** = μRT ln(P₁/P₂). Since ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas at constant T, Q = W: an isothermal expansion absorbs heat equal to the work it does.

**Adiabatic relation PV^γ = constant.** With dQ = 0, the first law gives 0 = μC_v dT + P dV. Differentiating PV = μRT gives P dV + V dP = μR dT. Eliminate dT and use C_p − C_v = R and γ = C_p/C_v; you get γ dV/V + dP/P = 0, which integrates to **PV^γ = constant**. Combining with PV = μRT also gives **TV^(γ−1) = constant** and **P^(1−γ)T^γ = constant**.

**Adiabatic work.** W = ∫ P dV with P = K/V^γ gives W = (P₁V₁ − P₂V₂)/(γ − 1) = **μR(T₁ − T₂)/(γ − 1)**. If the gas expands (T₂ < T₁), W is positive and comes entirely from internal energy.

**Why the adiabat is steeper:** the slope of an isotherm is dP/dV = −P/V; that of an adiabat is −γP/V. Since γ > 1, the adiabat falls faster.

**Isochoric and isobaric heat:** at constant volume Q = μC_vΔT (all to ΔU). At constant pressure Q = μC_pΔT, of which μC_vΔT raises U and μRΔT is work.

check.q: For a diatomic gas (γ = 1.4) compressed adiabatically to half its volume, the temperature is multiplied by about:
check.why: TV^(γ−1) is constant, so T₂/T₁ = (V₁/V₂)^0.4 = 2^0.4 ≈ 1.32.

sections.h: Free expansion, throttling and why irreversibility matters
sections.md:
Picture two identical vessels joined by a stopcock, one filled with gas, the other evacuated, all thermally insulated. Open the stopcock: the gas rushes into the empty vessel.

- No heat enters (insulated): Q = 0.
- The gas pushes against nothing: W = 0.
- So ΔU = 0, and for an ideal gas the temperature does not change.

Yet this is **not** a quasi-static adiabatic process — during the rush, pressure and temperature are not defined throughout the gas, so you cannot draw it on a P–V diagram, and PV^γ = constant does not apply. Final pressure is simply half the initial (Boyle's law between the end states).

And it never reverses on its own: the gas will not crowd back into one vessel. Free expansion is a textbook example of an **irreversible** process. Every irreversibility — friction, turbulence, heat flowing across a finite temperature gap — wastes the chance to do work, and that is exactly why real engines fall short of Carnot's limit.

**Did you know?** Your car's engine, an LPG cylinder's valve and even your refrigerator's expansion valve all involve irreversible steps. Engineers spend careers shaving these losses.

check.q: In the free expansion of an ideal gas into a vacuum (insulated), which is true?
options: Work done by gas is positive
check.why: Q = 0 and W = 0 because the gas expands against nothing, so ΔU = 0 and the ideal gas's temperature is unchanged.

sections.md:
1. **Heating water in a geyser** using fuel of known heat of combustion — energy needed m s ΔT, divided by heat per gram of fuel gives the fuel rate.
2. **Heating a gas at constant pressure** — Q = μC_pΔT; use C_p = (7/2)R for diatomic gases.
3. **Why two bodies at the same temperature need not hold the same heat** — heat is not stored; internal energy depends on mass and material.
4. **Path independence of adiabatic work** — if a gas goes from one state to another adiabatically by any route, W = −ΔU is the same.
5. **Work along a P–V path** — area of rectangles, triangles, trapeziums; sign by direction.
6. **Free expansion** — find final pressure and temperature.
7. **Engine/refrigerator energy bookkeeping** — W = Q₁ − Q₂, η, α.
8. **Carnot calculations** — always in kelvin.

parts.md: Raghav's mother put rice in the pressure cooker and walked off. 'Three whistles,' she called. Raghav, who had a physics test the next day, sat on the kitchen stool and watched. At first the lid stayed quiet: the cooker was sealed, the volume fixed — an isochoric process. Every joule from the flame went straight into internal energy. The pressure climbed and climbed.

Then the weight on the vent lifted and the first whistle shrieked. Steam rushed out through the tiny hole into the kitchen — not slowly, not quasi-statically; it roared. 'Irreversible,' Raghav muttered. The jet that hit the air felt cooler than he expected when he held his hand well away from it: the expanding steam had done work pushing the air aside and lost some internal energy, and it was quickly mixing with room air.

That night he drew it all: a vertical line on a P–V diagram for the heating, a messy unknown path for the whistle, heat Q₁ from the flame and heat lost to the kitchen. 'The kitchen is the cold reservoir,' he wrote, 'and the whistle is a terrible engine — all that energy and no work except noise.' The next day the test asked him to explain the first law with an everyday example. He smiled and drew a pressure cooker.

workedExamples.q: A geyser heats water flowing at 3.0 litres per minute from 27 °C to 77 °C. The fuel has a heat of combustion of 4.0 × 10⁴ J/g. At what rate is fuel consumed?
steps: Mass per minute = 3.0 kg (1 L of water ≈ 1 kg).
Heat per minute = m s ΔT = 3.0 × 4186 × 50 = 6.28 × 10⁵ J.

workedExamples.q: What amount of heat must be supplied to 2.0 × 10⁻² kg of nitrogen at room temperature to raise its temperature by 45 °C at constant pressure? (M = 28 g/mol, R = 8.3 J/mol K)

A system goes from A to B along a path in which 400 J of heat is absorbed and 150 J of work is done by the system. Along another path from A to B, 300 J of heat is absorbed. Find the work along the second path.
steps: ΔU is path-independent, so along path 2 ΔU = 250 J.

workedExamples.q: A gas expands adiabatically, doing 22.3 J of work. If instead it goes between the same two states by a different path absorbing 9.35 cal of heat, how much work is done on that path? (1 cal = 4.19 J)
workedExamples.answer: About 61.5 J done by the gas.

workedExamples.q: Two identical insulated cylinders joined by a stopcock: A holds an ideal gas at 1 atm, B is evacuated. The stopcock is opened. Find the final pressure and temperature change.
steps: Free expansion: Q = 0, W = 0, so ΔU = 0 and T is unchanged.
Volume doubles at constant T, so P = 1/2 atm by Boyle's law.

summary: Work done by a gas = area under its P–V curve; positive for expansion.
Net work in a cycle = enclosed area; clockwise = engine.
Heat and work depend on the path; ΔU does not.
Isothermal: W = μRT ln(V₂/V₁) = Q.
Adiabatic: PV^γ, TV^(γ−1) constant; W = μR(T₁ − T₂)/(γ − 1).
An adiabat is γ times steeper than an isotherm at the same point.
Free expansion: Q = W = ΔU = 0; irreversible; not on a P–V diagram.
At constant pressure Q = μC_pΔT; at constant volume Q = μC_vΔT.
Irreversibilities make real engines less efficient than Carnot.

rd-school-c11-physics-c.ch9-fluids.title: Mechanical Properties of Fluids
rd-school-c11-physics-c.ch9-fluids.subtitle: Pressure, flow, honey, soap bubbles — and the secret of how aeroplanes and spinning balls bend the air

sections.md:
Why does a dam get thicker towards its base? How does a mechanic lift a whole car with one hand on a hydraulic jack? Why does a spinning cricket ball swerve, and why do tiny water droplets on a lotus leaf stay round? All these questions belong to the physics of **fluids** — liquids and gases.

A fluid is a substance that **flows**. Unlike a solid, it has no fixed shape; it cannot sustain a shearing stress at rest — push a layer sideways and it just moves. Liquids are nearly incompressible and have a fixed volume; gases are highly compressible and fill their container.

In this chapter we study fluids at rest (**hydrostatics**: pressure, Pascal's law, buoyancy) and fluids in motion (**hydrodynamics**: streamlines, continuity, Bernoulli), then **viscosity** (fluid friction) and **surface tension** (the 'skin' of a liquid).

sections.h: Pressure and how it grows with depth
sections.md:
A sharp knife cuts; a blunt one doesn't, even with the same push. What matters is force **per unit area**:

**Pressure P = F / A**, a scalar, unit pascal (Pa = N/m²). Atmospheric pressure at sea level: **1 atm = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa**.

A fluid at rest pushes **perpendicular** to every surface it touches, and at a point the pressure is the same in all directions.

**Variation with depth**: consider a column of liquid of height h and area A. The extra weight ρ g h A must be supported by the extra pressure, so

**P = Pₐ + ρ g h**

where Pₐ is the atmospheric pressure on the surface. ρgh is the **gauge pressure** — what a tyre gauge or BP machine reads; P is the **absolute pressure**.

**Hydrostatic paradox**: the pressure at a given depth depends only on depth, not on the shape of the container. Connected vessels of different shapes fill to the same level.

That is why dams are thicker at the bottom: water pressure at 100 m depth is about 10 times atmospheric. Divers must ascend slowly; and your ears pop at the bottom of a deep swimming pool.

check.q: The gauge pressure 10 m below the surface of water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 m/s²) is:
check.why: ρgh = 1000 × 10 × 10 = 10⁵ Pa, about one extra atmosphere.

sections.md:
**Mercury barometer (Torricelli, 1643)**: fill a long glass tube with mercury and invert it in a dish of mercury. The column falls until its height is about **76 cm** at sea level, leaving near-vacuum above. The atmosphere's push on the dish balances the column: Pₐ = ρ_Hg g h. Hence the unit **mm of Hg** or **torr** (1 atm = 760 mm Hg). Doctors still measure blood pressure in mm Hg — '120/80' means gauge pressures of 120 and 80 mm Hg.

Why mercury? It is 13.6 times denser than water; a water barometer would need a tube about 10.3 m tall!

The **bar** (10⁵ Pa) and **millibar** are used in weather reports. A falling barometer often warns of a coming storm or cyclone.

**Open-tube manometer**: a U-tube with liquid; one end connected to the gas, the other open. The height difference h gives gauge pressure ρgh.

sections.h: Pascal's law and the hydraulic lift
sections.md:
**Pascal's law**: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted **undiminished** to every part of the fluid and the walls of its container.

This turns a small force into a huge one. In a **hydraulic lift**, a small piston of area A₁ is pushed with force F₁. The pressure F₁/A₁ reaches a large piston of area A₂, giving

**F₂ = F₁ × (A₂ / A₁)**

If A₂ is 100 times A₁, a 100 N push lifts 10,000 N — a small car. There's no free lunch: the small piston moves 100 times farther than the large one, so work in ≈ work out.

Uses: car-service jacks, **hydraulic brakes** (your foot on the pedal pressurises brake fluid that pushes all four wheel cylinders equally), JCB excavators, dentists' chairs, hydraulic presses for baling cotton.

fig.alt: Animated hydraulic lift: small piston pushes down, large piston raises a car.

check.q: In a hydraulic lift the pistons have areas 0.01 m² and 0.5 m². What force on the small piston lifts 20,000 N?

sections.h: Streamline flow and the equation of continuity
sections.md:
Watch smoke rising from an agarbatti. Near the stick it rises in smooth, parallel threads — **streamline (laminar) flow**. A little higher it breaks into swirls — **turbulent flow**.

In **steady flow**, the velocity at each point doesn't change with time. A **streamline** is the path traced by a fluid particle; the velocity is tangent to it. Streamlines never cross (otherwise a particle would have two velocities at once).

For an incompressible fluid, the mass entering one end of a pipe per second must leave the other end per second:

**A₁ v₁ = A₂ v₂** (**equation of continuity**)

It is conservation of mass. **Narrow pipe → faster flow.** Squeeze the end of a garden hose to make water shoot farther; rivers rush through narrow gorges and widen into slow, lazy plains.

When does flow become turbulent? When the **Reynolds number** Re = ρ v d / η exceeds about 2000 (below ~1000 the flow is streamline). High speed, wide pipes and low viscosity favour turbulence.

check.q: Water flows at 2 m/s in a pipe of area 10 cm². In a section of area 4 cm² its speed is:
check.why: v₂ = A₁v₁/A₂ = 10 × 2/4 = 5 m/s.

sections.md:
Daniel Bernoulli (1738) applied the work-energy theorem to a flowing fluid. Along a streamline, for steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow:

**P + ½ ρ v² + ρ g h = constant**

In words: pressure energy + kinetic energy + potential energy per unit volume is constant. Where the fluid **speeds up**, its **pressure drops**.

**Speed of efflux (Torricelli's law)**: water leaking from a hole a depth h below the open surface of a tank emerges with **v = √(2gh)** — the same as free fall from height h.

**Venturi meter**: a pipe with a narrow throat. Faster flow at the throat means lower pressure there; the pressure difference (read with a manometer) tells you the flow rate. Your car's carburettor, a scent sprayer and the Bunsen burner all use this.

**Blood flow**: if an artery narrows due to plaque, blood speeds up and pressure drops there, which can make the artery partially collapse — a reason doctors take narrowing seriously.

**Dynamic lift**: an aerofoil (wing) is shaped and tilted so air flows faster over the top, lowering pressure there; the pressure difference lifts the wing. A spinning ball drags air around with it; the side where spin adds to airflow has faster air and lower pressure, so the ball curves — the **Magnus effect**, seen in a spinner's drift or a swinging football free kick.

Warning signs: fast trains rushing past a platform lower the pressure between the train and you — stand behind the yellow line!

check.q: Water flows out of a small hole 5 m below the water surface of a large open tank (g = 10 m/s²). Speed of efflux:

sections.md:
Pour honey and water side by side. Honey crawls. The internal friction between layers of a moving fluid is **viscosity**.

When a liquid flows over a surface, the layer touching it is at rest and successive layers move faster. The force needed to keep layers sliding is

**F = η A (dv/dx)**

where η (eta) is the **coefficient of viscosity**, SI unit **pascal second (Pa s)** — also called poiseuille. Water ≈ 10⁻³ Pa s, blood ≈ 3–4 × 10⁻³, glycerine ≈ 1.5, honey a few Pa s.

Viscosity of liquids **decreases with temperature** (hot ghee pours easily, cold ghee doesn't); viscosity of gases **increases** with temperature.

**Stokes' law**: a small sphere of radius a moving at speed v through a viscous fluid feels drag **F = 6π η a v**. A falling sphere accelerates until drag + buoyancy balance weight, reaching **terminal velocity**:

**v_t = 2 a² (ρ − σ) g / 9η**

(ρ = sphere density, σ = fluid density). Tiny raindrops fall gently because v_t ∝ a² — and a parachute raises drag to keep landing speed safe.

check.q: If the radius of a falling droplet doubles, its terminal velocity becomes:
check.why: v_t ∝ a², so doubling the radius makes the terminal velocity 2² = 4 times larger.

sections.md:
A steel needle can float on water. Insects called water striders walk on ponds. Raindrops are round. A liquid surface behaves like a **stretched elastic membrane** — this is **surface tension**.

**Why?** A molecule inside a liquid is pulled equally by neighbours in all directions. A molecule at the surface has neighbours only below and beside it, so it has **extra energy**. Creating more surface costs energy; the liquid minimises its surface area — and for a given volume, the sphere has the least area.

**Surface tension S** = force per unit length acting along the surface = **surface energy per unit area**. Units: N/m or J/m². Water at 20 °C: about 0.073 N/m. It decreases as temperature rises; detergent and soap lower it a lot (which is why soapy water wets greasy cloth better).

**Angle of contact θ**: where a liquid meets a solid, the angle between the liquid surface and the solid. Water on clean glass: θ < 90° — it **wets** the glass and spreads. Mercury on glass, or water on a waxy lotus leaf: θ > 90° — it forms beads.

**Drops and bubbles**: the pressure inside is greater than outside:
- Liquid drop: **Pᵢ − Pₒ = 2S / r**
- Soap bubble (two surfaces): **Pᵢ − Pₒ = 4S / r**

Smaller bubbles have *higher* inside pressure.

**Capillary rise**: water climbs up a thin glass tube to height **h = 2S cos θ / (ρ g a)**, where a is the tube radius. Thinner tubes give higher rise. Mercury (θ > 90°) is pushed *down*. Capillary action helps water rise in a cotton wick, blotting paper and the soil.

sections.h: Bernoulli at work: Torricelli's law and the venturimeter
sections.md:
Part 1 stated Bernoulli's principle: along a streamline of an ideal fluid (incompressible, non-viscous, steady flow), **P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant**. Each term is an energy per unit volume — pressure energy, kinetic energy and potential energy. Now let us use it.

**Speed of efflux (Torricelli's law).** A tank open to the air has a small hole at depth h below the water surface. Apply Bernoulli between the surface (pressure P_a, speed nearly zero because the tank is wide) and the hole (pressure P_a, speed v): P_a + ρgh = P_a + ½ρv², so **v = √(2gh)** — the same speed a stone would gain falling freely through h. If the tank is closed with gas at pressure P above the water, v = √(2(P − P_a)/ρ + 2gh).

**Venturimeter.** A pipe narrows from area A₁ to a throat of area A₂. By continuity, v₂ = v₁A₁/A₂ is larger in the throat; by Bernoulli, pressure there is lower. A U-tube manometer between the wide part and the throat shows a height difference h of the manometer liquid (density ρ_m), giving P₁ − P₂ = ρ_m g h = ½ρv₁²[(A₁/A₂)² − 1]. Measure h, compute v₁ — this is how flow is metered in pipelines and how a car carburettor's throat sucks in petrol.

**Did you know?** The **atomiser** (perfume spray, a mosquito-repellent sprayer or a paint gun) works the same way: fast air over the tube top lowers pressure, and the liquid rises and breaks into droplets.

sections.h: Lift, swing and blood: more Bernoulli stories
sections.md:
**Dynamic lift on a wing.** An aerofoil is shaped and tilted so that air flows faster over the top than under the bottom. Faster flow means lower pressure on top; the pressure difference times the wing area gives an upward **dynamic lift**. (Deflection of air downwards — Newton's third law — is the other half of the same story.)

**Magnus effect — the spinning ball.** A ball moving through air while spinning drags a thin layer of air round with it. On the side where the ball's surface moves the same way as the air streaming past it, the air speed is increased; on the other side it is reduced. The faster side has lower pressure, so the ball curves towards it. A ball with backspin (top surface moving backwards, with the air) gets an upward lift; topspin makes it dip sharply. That is why a spinner can make a cricket ball drift and dip and a footballer can bend a free kick. (Conventional swing of a new cricket ball also involves the seam and a shiny vs rough side, which makes the air layer separate differently — a more advanced effect.)

**Blood flow and heart attack.** When an artery narrows because of plaque on its inner wall, blood must speed up through the constriction, and by Bernoulli the pressure there drops. The external pressure can then partially collapse the soft artery; the heart has to work harder to push blood through. (This is a physics illustration only; medical questions need a doctor.)

**Roofs in a storm.** A cyclone blowing fast over a flat roof lowers the pressure above it, while still air inside keeps normal pressure — the roof can be lifted off. Opening windows slightly equalises pressure.

check.q: A ball has backspin: its top surface moves backwards, in the same direction as the air streaming past it. The ball tends to:
check.why: The top surface drags air along with the stream, so air moves faster over the top, pressure there is lower, and the ball is lifted.

sections.h: Viscosity in depth: Stokes' law, terminal velocity and Reynolds number
sections.md:
Real fluids have **viscosity**, internal friction between layers. For a layer-to-layer velocity gradient v/l, the viscous force on area A is F = ηA(v/l), where η is the **coefficient of viscosity** (SI unit Pa s, also called poiseuille; the CGS unit is the poise, 1 poise = 0.1 Pa s). Water at 20 °C has η ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa s; blood about 2.7 × 10⁻³ (at 37 °C); glycerine about 0.83; honey far higher. Viscosity of liquids **falls** with temperature (warm honey pours easily), while that of gases **rises**.

**Stokes' law.** A small sphere of radius a moving at speed v through a viscous fluid feels a drag **F = 6πηav**.

**Terminal velocity.** Drop a steel ball into a tall jar of glycerine (or think of a raindrop). It accelerates until weight = buoyancy + viscous drag, then falls at constant **terminal velocity**: (4/3)πa³ρg = (4/3)πa³σg + 6πηav_t, so

**v_t = 2a²(ρ − σ)g / (9η)**, where ρ is the sphere's density and σ the fluid's.

Bigger drops fall faster (v_t ∝ a²): drizzle floats, monsoon downpours pelt. Millikan used exactly this for oil drops to measure the electron's charge. If σ > ρ (an air bubble in water), v_t is negative — the bubble rises.

**Reynolds number.** Whether flow stays smooth or becomes turbulent depends on **R_e = ρvd/η** (d = pipe diameter). Below about 1000, flow is streamline; above about 2000, turbulent; in between, unsteady. Turbulence wastes energy as heat — but it helps mixing, and golf balls are dimpled to trigger it and fly farther.

check.q: If the radius of a falling raindrop doubles, its terminal velocity becomes:
check.why: v_t ∝ a², so doubling the radius makes the terminal velocity 2² = 4 times.

sections.h: Surface tension in depth: energy, contact angle, drops and bubbles
sections.md:
A molecule deep in a liquid is pulled equally in all directions; one at the surface is pulled inward. Bringing a molecule to the surface costs energy, so a liquid surface stores **surface energy**. **Surface tension S** is the force per unit length along any line in the surface, and it equals the surface energy per unit area (unit N/m = J/m²). Water at 20 °C: about 0.0727 N/m; mercury about 0.465 N/m; soap solution about 0.03 N/m. S falls as temperature rises.

**Angle of contact θ.** Where a liquid meets a solid, the liquid surface meets the solid at angle θ. If the liquid wets the solid (water on clean glass), θ < 90° and the meniscus is concave. If not (mercury on glass, water on a waxy lotus leaf), θ > 90° and drops bead up. **Detergents and soaps** lower S and reduce θ so water wets greasy cloth and lifts dirt; **waterproofing** agents raise θ.

**Excess pressure inside curved surfaces.** Surface tension squeezes a drop, so the inside is at higher pressure:

- Liquid drop or a bubble inside a liquid (one surface): **ΔP = 2S/r**.
- Soap bubble in air (two surfaces): **ΔP = 4S/r**.

Smaller bubbles have higher pressure — connect a small and a large soap bubble by a tube and the small one shrinks into the big one!

**Capillary rise.** In a thin glass tube of radius a, water rises to height **h = 2S cos θ/(ρga)**. Thinner tubes, higher rise. Mercury (θ > 90°) is depressed instead. Capillarity helps water move up soil and into a cotton wick of a diya; it is one part of how water rises in plants.

**Did you know?** A water strider walks on ponds and a steel needle carefully laid on water floats — surface tension supports them, though they are denser than water.

2. **Hydraulic lift / brakes** — F₂ = F₁A₂/A₁; work in = work out.
3. **Manometer and barometer columns** — mercury vs water heights; liquids of different densities in a U-tube.

rd-school-c11-physics-d.ch12-kinetic-the.title: Kinetic Theory
rd-school-c11-physics-d.ch12-kinetic-the.subtitle: Billions of tiny molecules, crashing about at the speed of a bullet — and out of the chaos, simple laws

sections.h: The invisible storm in a room
sections.md:
Right now, the air around you is a furious storm. Nitrogen and oxygen molecules are flying at roughly **500 m/s** — faster than a rifle bullet — colliding with each other billions of times every second, and drumming on your skin. You feel this drumming as **air pressure**. When someone opens a bottle of attar across the room, its smell reaches you because those molecules wander through this storm.

The **kinetic theory of gases** explains the behaviour of gases (pressure, temperature, specific heat, diffusion) in terms of the motion of molecules. It connects the macroscopic world of thermodynamics with the microscopic world of atoms. Developed in the 19th century by Clausius, Maxwell and Boltzmann, it was one of the first strong pieces of evidence that atoms are real.

Here we follow the chapter's story: molecular nature of matter → behaviour of gases → kinetic theory of an ideal gas → law of equipartition of energy → specific heats → mean free path.

The idea that matter is made of indivisible particles is ancient. In India, the philosopher **Kanada** (of the Vaisheshika school) spoke of *paramanu*, the smallest particles of matter; in Greece, **Democritus** used the word *atomos*. These were philosophical ideas, not experimental.

The scientific atomic theory came with **John Dalton** (early 1800s), who explained the laws of definite and multiple proportions in chemistry. **Gay-Lussac's law** (gases combine in simple volume ratios) and **Avogadro's law** (equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules) followed.

Key numbers:
- **Avogadro number N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ per mole.**
- Size of an atom: about 1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m.
- In a solid, atoms are packed a few Å apart; in a gas at room conditions, they are tens of Å apart, so a gas is mostly empty space.

A molecule in a gas travels a distance called the **mean free path** between collisions — thousands of times its own size at normal pressure.

sections.h: Behaviour of gases: the ideal-gas law
sections.md:
At low pressure and high temperature, all gases obey

**PV = μRT = N k_B T**

where μ is the number of moles, N the number of molecules, **R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹** and **k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K** (Boltzmann's constant).

It contains the older laws:
- **Boyle's law**: at fixed T, PV = constant.
- **Charles' law**: at fixed P, V ∝ T.
- **Avogadro**: at fixed P and T, V ∝ N. One mole of any ideal gas occupies **22.4 L at STP** (273 K, 1 atm).

**Dalton's law of partial pressures**: in a mixture of non-reacting ideal gases, the total pressure is the sum of the pressures each gas would exert alone: P = P₁ + P₂ + ….

Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature, where molecules come close and attract each other; they approach ideal behaviour as density falls.

sections.h: Kinetic theory of an ideal gas
sections.md:
**Assumptions** (the model):
1. A gas consists of a very large number of identical molecules in random motion.
2. Molecules are tiny compared with the spaces between them — their own volume is negligible.
3. They exert no forces on each other except during collisions.
4. Collisions with each other and the walls are perfectly elastic and last a negligible time.
5. Newton's laws apply to each molecule.

**Pressure from collisions**: a molecule of mass m with velocity component vx hits a wall and rebounds with −vx; momentum transferred = 2m vx. Counting how many such hits per second strike area A, and averaging (by symmetry ⟨vx²⟩ = ⟨v²⟩/3), we get

**P = ⅓ n m ⟨v²⟩**

where n is the number of molecules per unit volume. Since nm = ρ (density), **P = ⅓ ρ ⟨v²⟩**.

The pressure of a gas is literally the averaged rain of molecular impacts.

sections.md:
Compare the kinetic-theory result with the gas law. PV = ⅓ N m ⟨v²⟩ = ⅔ N (½ m ⟨v²⟩), and PV = N k_B T. Therefore

**average kinetic energy of a molecule = ½ m ⟨v²⟩ = (3/2) k_B T**

This is a profound result: **temperature is a measure of the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules.** It doesn't depend on pressure, volume or the type of gas — at the same temperature, a heavy CO₂ molecule and a light H₂ molecule have the *same* average kinetic energy (H₂ just moves faster).

The **root mean square speed**:

**v_rms = √⟨v²⟩ = √(3 k_B T / m) = √(3RT / M)** (M = molar mass in kg/mol)

For oxygen at 300 K: √(3 × 8.31 × 300/0.032) ≈ **483 m/s**. For hydrogen, four times lighter per atom-pair ratio (M = 0.002), it is about 1930 m/s. Light hydrogen and helium escape more easily from Earth's gravity over geological time — which is why our atmosphere has so little of them.

At the same T, v_rms ∝ 1/√M. That idea underlies **Graham's law of diffusion** and the separation of uranium isotopes in gaseous form.

check.q: If the absolute temperature of a gas is made four times, v_rms becomes:
check.why: v_rms ∝ √T, and √4 = 2.

sections.md:
A molecule can store energy in different independent ways, called **degrees of freedom (f)**:
- **Translational**: moving along x, y, z — 3 degrees for any molecule.
- **Rotational**: a diatomic molecule (like O₂, dumb-bell shaped) can rotate about 2 axes perpendicular to its bond — 2 more.
- **Vibrational**: atoms in a molecule can vibrate along the bond, adding kinetic + potential terms (2 more per mode), but this only 'switches on' at higher temperatures.

**Law of equipartition of energy**: in thermal equilibrium, the total energy is shared equally among all available degrees of freedom; each degree of freedom (each quadratic term) has average energy **½ k_B T**.

| Gas | f (room temp.) | Energy per molecule |
|---|---|---|
| Monatomic (He, Ar) | 3 | (3/2) k_B T |
| Diatomic rigid (O₂, N₂) | 5 | (5/2) k_B T |
| Diatomic with vibration | 7 | (7/2) k_B T |
| Polyatomic non-linear (rigid) | 6 | 3 k_B T |

check.q: A rigid diatomic molecule at room temperature has how many degrees of freedom?
check.why: It has 3 translational and 2 rotational degrees of freedom; vibration is usually frozen out at room temperature.

sections.h: Specific heat capacities from kinetic theory
sections.md:
Equipartition predicts specific heats.

**Monatomic gas**: U = (3/2) R T per mole ⇒ **Cv = (3/2) R**, Cp = Cv + R = (5/2) R, **γ = 5/3 ≈ 1.67**.

**Rigid diatomic gas**: U = (5/2) R T ⇒ **Cv = (5/2) R**, Cp = (7/2) R, **γ = 7/5 = 1.4**. With vibration active: Cv = (7/2)R, γ = 9/7 ≈ 1.29.

**Polyatomic gas** with f_rot = 3 and v vibrational modes: Cv = (3 + f)R... in general Cv = (f/2)R and **γ = 1 + 2/f**.

These predictions match experiment well for most gases, which was a huge triumph.

**Solids**: each atom vibrates in 3 dimensions, with kinetic + potential terms — 6 quadratic terms — so U = 3RT per mole and **C = 3R ≈ 25 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹** (the **Dulong–Petit law**). Most metals at room temperature obey this.

**Water**: treating each of the 3 atoms like an atom in a solid gives about 9R ≈ 75 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ — close to water's actual 75.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Where classical theory fails — at low temperatures, specific heats fall towards zero — quantum mechanics is needed: some degrees of freedom 'freeze'.

sections.md:
If molecules fly at 500 m/s, why does the smell of a lit agarbatti take several seconds or more to cross a room? Because each molecule collides constantly and changes direction — it follows a zig-zag **random walk**.

The average distance a molecule travels between collisions is the **mean free path**:

**l = 1 / (√2 n π d²)**

where n is the number density and d the molecular diameter. A molecule sweeps a 'collision cylinder' of radius d; the √2 accounts for the motion of the other molecules too.

For air at STP: n ≈ 2.7 × 10²⁵ m⁻³ and d ≈ 3 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, giving l of the order of **10⁻⁷ m** (around a hundred nanometres) — hundreds of times the molecular diameter. Molecules collide billions of times per second.

At lower pressure n falls, so l grows: in high vacuum tubes or the upper atmosphere, it can be centimetres to kilometres.

The random-walk picture explains **diffusion** (slow spreading of a smell or of ink in water) and **Brownian motion** — the jittery dance of pollen grains or smoke particles hit unevenly by molecules, first explained quantitatively by Einstein in 1905.

rd-school-c11-physics-d.ch12-kinetic-the.title: Kinetic Theory — Part 2: Derivations, Speeds, Specific Heats & Every Exercise Type
rd-school-c11-physics-d.ch12-kinetic-the.subtitle: From a molecule hitting a wall to why helium escapes Earth — the chapter's maths made friendly

sections.h: Deriving the pressure of an ideal gas
sections.md:
Part 1 stated the result P = ⅓ n m v̄² (n = molecules per unit volume). Here is where it comes from — a favourite long answer.

**Assumptions of kinetic theory:** a gas is a huge number of identical molecules; they are point-like (their own volume is negligible); they move randomly in all directions; they do not attract or repel except during collisions; collisions with each other and with walls are perfectly elastic; and between collisions they move in straight lines at constant speed.

**Step 1 — one molecule, one wall.** Take a cube of side l. A molecule with velocity (v_x, v_y, v_z) hits the wall perpendicular to x. Elastic collision reverses v_x: momentum change = −2mv_x for the molecule, so +2mv_x is given to the wall.

**Step 2 — how often?** In time Δt, molecules within distance v_xΔt of the wall and moving towards it will hit it. In area A that is a volume Av_xΔt containing nAv_xΔt molecules, of which half move towards the wall. Momentum delivered = ½ nAv_xΔt × 2mv_x = nmv_x²AΔt.

**Step 3 — pressure.** Force/area = momentum per time per area: P = nmv_x². Molecules have different speeds, so use the average: P = nm⟨v_x²⟩.

**Step 4 — isotropy.** No direction is special, so ⟨v_x²⟩ = ⟨v_y²⟩ = ⟨v_z²⟩ = ⅓⟨v²⟩. Hence **P = ⅓ nm⟨v²⟩ = ⅓ ρ⟨v²⟩**.

Collisions between molecules do not change the result: they swap momentum among molecules but, in a steady state, the average stays the same. Neither does the container's shape.

**Link to temperature.** PV = ⅓Nm⟨v²⟩ = ⅔N(½m⟨v²⟩). Comparing with PV = Nk_BT gives the key result **average translational KE per molecule = (3/2)k_BT**, with k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K.

sections.h: Molecular speeds, Dalton's law and Graham's law
sections.md:
From ½m⟨v²⟩ = (3/2)k_BT we get the **root-mean-square speed**

**v_rms = √(3k_BT/m) = √(3RT/M)** (M = molar mass in kg/mol).

For nitrogen at 300 K: √(3 × 8.31 × 300/0.028) = √(2.67 × 10⁵) ≈ 517 m/s — faster than a passenger jet. Hydrogen, 14 times lighter, is √14 ≈ 3.7 times faster.

Speeds in a gas are spread out — some molecules slow, some fast (the **Maxwell distribution**). The rms speed is one convenient average.

**Why the Moon and lighter planets lose gases:** escape speed from Earth is about 11.2 km/s. Even a small fraction of hydrogen and helium molecules at the high-altitude temperature move fast enough to escape over millions of years, which is why our atmosphere holds little of either. The Moon, with escape speed 2.4 km/s, has kept almost no atmosphere.

**Dalton's law of partial pressures.** For a mixture, P = ⅓n₁m₁⟨v₁²⟩ + ⅓n₂m₂⟨v₂²⟩ + … = P₁ + P₂ + …. Each gas pushes as if it were alone. In equilibrium all components share the same average KE per molecule.

**Graham's law of diffusion.** Lighter molecules diffuse faster: rate ∝ 1/√M. This was used to separate uranium isotopes: ²³⁵UF₆ and ²³⁸UF₆ differ in molar mass by just 3 parts in 352, so the diffusion rate ratio is √(352/349) ≈ 1.0043 — the process has to be repeated through thousands of stages.

**Avogadro's hypothesis follows:** equal volumes of gases at the same T and P have the same number of molecules, since PV = Nk_BT does not depend on the kind of gas. One mole occupies 22.4 L at STP.

check.q: At the same temperature, the ratio v_rms(He)/v_rms(Ar) (M = 4 and 40 g/mol) is:
check.why: v_rms ∝ 1/√M, so the ratio is √(40/4) = √10 ≈ 3.16.

sections.h: Degrees of freedom and equipartition — the full table
sections.md:
A **degree of freedom** is an independent way a molecule can hold energy. The **law of equipartition** says that in thermal equilibrium each quadratic energy term (½mv_x², ½Iω², ½kx²…) carries on average **½k_BT** per molecule.

| Molecule | Translational | Rotational | Vibrational (if active) | U per mole | C_v | C_p | γ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Monatomic (He, Ar) | 3 | 0 | 0 | (3/2)RT | (3/2)R | (5/2)R | 5/3 ≈ 1.67 |
| Diatomic rigid (O₂, N₂ at room T) | 3 | 2 | 0 | (5/2)RT | (5/2)R | (7/2)R | 7/5 = 1.40 |
| Diatomic with vibration (high T) | 3 | 2 | 1 mode = 2 terms | (7/2)RT | (7/2)R | (9/2)R | 9/7 ≈ 1.29 |
| Polyatomic (f vibrational modes) | 3 | 3 | f modes | (3 + f)RT | (3 + f)R | (4 + f)R | (4 + f)/(3 + f) |

Why does a vibrational mode count twice? A vibrating bond has both kinetic energy (½m v²) and potential energy (½k x²) — two quadratic terms, so k_BT per molecule.

Why only 2 rotations for a diatomic? Rotation about the bond axis has a negligible moment of inertia, so it stores no energy at ordinary temperatures.

**Limits of classical theory:** at low temperatures measured specific heats fall below these predictions, because rotational and vibrational modes "freeze out". Explaining that needed quantum mechanics.

check.q: For a mixture of 1 mole helium and 1 mole oxygen (rigid), C_v of the mixture per mole is:
check.why: Total C_v = (3/2)R + (5/2)R = 4R for 2 moles, i.e. 2R per mole of mixture.

sections.h: Specific heat of solids and water; Brownian motion
sections.md:
**Solids (Dulong–Petit law).** Treat each atom of a solid as an oscillator vibrating in 3 directions. Each direction has KE and PE terms, so 2 × ½k_BT = k_BT per direction, 3k_BT per atom. Per mole, U = 3RT, so **C = 3R ≈ 25 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹**. Aluminium (24.4), copper (24.5), silver (24.9), lead (26.4) agree well; carbon in diamond (6.1) does not, because its stiff bonds keep vibrations frozen at room temperature — again a quantum effect.

**Water.** Treating a water molecule like a solid's three-atom unit gives about 9R ≈ 75 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, i.e. 75/0.018 ≈ 4170 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ — remarkably close to the measured 4186. That is why the rough model is quoted in the textbook.

**Brownian motion.** In 1827 Robert Brown saw pollen grains jiggling endlessly in water under a microscope. The jiggling is caused by unbalanced, random impacts of water molecules on the tiny grain. Smaller particles, less viscous liquids and higher temperatures give livelier motion. Einstein's 1905 analysis of it let Perrin measure Avogadro's number, finally convincing sceptics that atoms are real. You can see similar motion in smoke particles lit by a sunbeam in a dark room.

check.q: According to the Dulong–Petit law, the molar specific heat of most solids is about:
check.why: Each atom vibrates in three directions, each with KE and PE, giving 3k_BT per atom and 3R per mole.

sections.h: Mean free path in more detail
sections.md:
Molecules collide with each other constantly. Model each as a sphere of diameter d. A molecule moving at speed ⟨v⟩ sweeps out, in time t, a cylinder of cross-section πd² and length ⟨v⟩t; any molecule whose centre lies inside it gets hit. The number of collisions is n πd²⟨v⟩t, so the average distance between collisions is 1/(nπd²). Allowing for the fact that the other molecules are also moving gives

**ℓ = 1/(√2 n π d²)**.

For air at STP, n ≈ 2.7 × 10²⁵ m⁻³ and d ≈ 3 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, so ℓ ≈ 1/(1.41 × 2.7 × 10²⁵ × 3.14 × 9 × 10⁻²⁰) ≈ 9 × 10⁻⁸ m, about 300 molecular diameters. At ~500 m/s that is several billion collisions per second for each molecule.

This explains why a perfume opened in one corner takes many seconds — not milliseconds — to reach you: each molecule zigzags randomly. In a high vacuum (a TV tube or a particle accelerator) n is tiny and ℓ can be metres or more.

workedExamples.answer: About 10⁻⁴ — gas is mostly empty space.
